questions.title: Floor of the inguinal canal
questions.question: A 54 years old male suffered from a scrotal swelling that increases with cough and sneezing. On examination, it was diagnosed as inguinal hernia that passes through the inguinal canal. Which one of the following forms the floor of this structure?
questions.subject: msk

explanations.A: Incorrect. The arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis form the roof of the inguinal canal, not the floor — the opposite wall from the one this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medially, not the floor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fascia transversalis forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon); it is not the floor.
explanations.D: Correct. The floor of the inguinal canal is the inguinal ligament — the rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, stretching from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle — reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament. This ligamentous floor is the wall the canal's contents rest on as they pass from the deep to the superficial inguinal ring.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Medial fibers of internal oblique reinforce the anterior wall of the inguinal canal (alongside the external oblique aponeurosis), not the floor.

questions.learning_objective: Name the inguinal (and lacunar) ligament as the floor of the inguinal canal, distinct from its anterior, posterior and roof walls.

questions.title: Which is NOT a function of calcium
questions.question: Regarding function of calcium one of these is incorrect:
questions.subject: fnd

options.B: is a constituent of bone and teath
options.E: essential for the activity of lipase

explanations.A: Correct (the incorrect statement, and so the answer). The department's own taught list of calcium's functions names lipase and phosphorylase as the enzymes calcium activates — it does not include acting as a coenzyme of a kinase. Calcium works in these enzymatic roles as a cofactor/activator, and "coenzyme of a kinase" is not part of the specific list this exam is built on.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true statement, so not the answer). Calcium is genuinely a structural constituent of bone and teeth — about 99% of body calcium is stored in the skeleton for exactly this reason.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Calcium genuinely regulates nerve impulse transmission and neuromuscular excitability, which is why a fall in the physiologically active (ionized) fraction of plasma calcium precipitates tetany.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Calcium is genuinely essential for blood and milk clotting, named directly among the department's taught functions of calcium.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). The department book names lipase specifically as one of the enzymes whose activity requires calcium, alongside phosphorylase — this is a true, taught function, unlike option A's kinase claim.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the department's five taught functions of calcium and recognise that a kinase-coenzyme role is not among them.

questions.title: Calcitonin's action on bone in remodeling
questions.question: In bone remodling, calcitonin,
questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stimulating osteoclasts would promote bone resorption, the opposite of calcitonin's taught action — calcitonin inhibits, rather than stimulates, the mobilization of calcium from bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Promoting bone resorption is parathyroid hormone's action (which mobilises calcium from bone to raise plasma calcium), not calcitonin's — calcitonin's action on bone is the reverse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increasing calcium/phosphate release from bone describes resorption, which calcitonin suppresses rather than causes; this option describes the opposite of the department's taught calcitonin action.
explanations.D: Correct. The department book states that by inhibiting mobilization of calcium from the bones, calcitonin decreases plasma calcium level — i.e. calcitonin suppresses bone resorption. This is the direct opposite of parathyroid hormone's bone-mobilizing action, and is why calcitonin lowers rather than raises plasma calcium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Inhibiting calcium absorption describes an intestinal action, not calcitonin's taught bone action; calcitonin's role as taught is specifically on bone (suppressing resorption), not on intestinal absorption.

questions.learning_objective: State that calcitonin lowers plasma calcium by suppressing (inhibiting) bone resorption, opposite to parathyroid hormone's action.

questions.title: Protein defect underlying Menkes disease (Group 2 wording)
questions.question: Menkes disease is caused by defect in:
questions.subject: fnd

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibronectin is a distinct extracellular-matrix adhesion glycoprotein, unrelated to the copper-transport/lysyl-oxidase pathway defective in Menkes disease.
explanations.B: Correct. Menkes disease is a copper-transport defect that starves the copper-dependent enzyme lysyl oxidase, which is responsible for cross-linking collagen (and, by the same chemistry, elastin) after secretion. As tested and taught on this exam paper, the resulting defect is named as a collagen defect, reflecting lysyl oxidase's essential cross-linking role in collagen maturation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Laminin is a basement-membrane glycoprotein unrelated to lysyl-oxidase-mediated cross-linking; it plays no role in Menkes disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fibrillin-1 is the gene defective in Marfan syndrome, a separate extracellular-matrix disorder involving a structural scaffold protein rather than the copper-dependent cross-linking enzyme defective in Menkes disease.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Elastin is, like collagen, a substrate that lysyl oxidase normally cross-links, and both are affected by the enzyme's copper starvation in Menkes disease — but as printed and keyed on this paper, the tested answer names collagen rather than elastin as the affected protein.

questions.learning_objective: State that Menkes disease is a copper-transport defect that impairs lysyl-oxidase-mediated collagen cross-linking.

questions.title: Definition of the sarcomere
questions.question: The sarcomere is the distance between two successive:
questions.subject: msk

explanations.A: Incorrect. The A band is the dark band formed by overlapping thick and thin filaments; a sarcomere includes one entire A band (plus half of the I band on each side), but the sarcomere is not defined as the distance between two A bands.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The H zone is the lighter central region of the A band where only thick filaments lie (no overlap); it is a sub-region within a single sarcomere's A band, not the landmark whose repeat distance defines a sarcomere.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The I band is the light band of thin filaments only, bisected by the Z line; a sarcomere is built from half an I band on each side of its A band, but is not itself measured as the distance between two I bands.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The M line is the midline of the A band (and of the whole sarcomere), not the boundary marker between successive sarcomeres — a sarcomere runs Z-line to Z-line with the M line at its centre, not M-line to M-line by definition.
explanations.E: Correct. The sarcomere, the functional contractile unit of the skeletal muscle fiber, is defined as the distance between two successive Z lines — spanning one complete A band plus half of the I band on each side. As a muscle contracts, Z lines move closer together while the A band's length stays constant, which is why Z-line spacing (not any other band's) is what measures sarcomere shortening.

questions.learning_objective: Define the sarcomere as the distance between two successive Z lines.

questions.title: T-tubule equivalent in smooth muscle cells
questions.question: In smooth muscle cells, which of the following represents T- tubules?
questions.subject: msk

explanations.A: Incorrect. Attachment plaques are small, darkly staining patches on the sarcolemma where dense bodies containing alpha-actinin anchor actin filaments — they play the anchoring role the Z line plays in skeletal muscle, not the impulse-conducting role of T tubules.
explanations.B: Correct. Smooth muscle has no true T-tubule system. The histology department book states that subsarcolemmal caveolae — vesicular invaginations of the sarcolemma — function like T tubules in conducting the contraction impulse, and, together with the poorly developed sarcoplasmic reticulum, help regulate calcium flow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dense bodies are cytoplasmic (and membrane-attached) structures that anchor actin filaments in smooth muscle, functionally analogous to the Z line's anchoring role — not a T-tubule equivalent for impulse conduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Desmin is a cytoskeletal intermediate filament protein that helps link dense bodies together and to the cytoskeleton; it is a structural scaffolding protein, not a membrane structure that conducts the contraction impulse.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Gap junctions (nexuses) electrically couple adjacent smooth muscle cells, allowing impulse spread from cell to cell — a different function from a T tubule's role of conducting the impulse into the interior of a single cell.

questions.learning_objective: State that caveolae are the taught structural/functional equivalent of T tubules in smooth muscle, which itself lacks a true T-tubule system.

questions.title: Cause of rigor mortis stiffness (Group 2 wording)
questions.question: A cadaver discovered two days after death showing Rigor Mortis Signs in the form of Stiffening of the joints and muscles. What is the cause of the stifness?
questions.subject: msk

options.A: ATP, which is necessary for the detachment of cross bridges, is not being formed.
options.B: ATP, which is necessary for formation of cross bridges, continues to be formed after death.
options.C: ATP, which is necessary for the formation of cross bridges, is not being formed.
options.D: Deterioration of muscle proteins prevents detachment of cross bridges.
options.E: Deterioration of muscle proteins causes detachment of cross bridges.

explanations.A: Correct. ATP is required for the myosin cross bridge to detach from actin after the power stroke, not only to form it. After death, ATP production stops, so cross bridges that have already attached to exposed actin sites (with calcium pumps also failing) cannot release — this failure of ATP-dependent detachment, not formation, is what produces the sustained rigidity of rigor mortis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ATP production stops after death rather than continuing — this option's premise (ATP continuing to be formed) is the opposite of what actually happens and does not explain rigidity in any case, since it is detachment, not formation, that ATP is needed for in this mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This option correctly notes that ATP is not being formed after death but wrongly claims ATP is needed for cross-bridge formation — cross bridges still form (myosin still binds the exposed actin sites); it is their detachment, not their formation, that specifically requires ATP and fails.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deterioration of muscle proteins is what eventually resolves rigor mortis (by breaking down the bound cross bridges), not what causes it in the first place — the cause is ATP depletion preventing detachment, occurring well before protein deterioration begins.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Deterioration of muscle proteins, when it does occur, breaks down (releases) cross bridges and so resolves rigor mortis rather than causing detachment as part of the stiffening process — this option both mistimes and reverses the role of protein deterioration.

questions.learning_objective: State that rigor mortis results from ATP depletion preventing actin-myosin cross-bridge detachment (not formation), and that protein deterioration only later resolves it.
